$doc: Vyomi capability registry — GCP Cloud Run functions (the real console folds /functions into Cloud Run; this registry covers every section of that console page set). Proven by tests/conformance/test_capabilities.py — a claim the backend does not honour fails CI.

gcp.functions.services.scaling_billing.title: Service scaling, ingress and CPU allocation (request-based / instance-based billing)
limitations: Billing is not metered; the console mirrors the cpuIdle setting but Vyomi does not charge for instance time.

gcp.functions.services.source.title: Source (inline function entry point, runtime, code)
limitations: "Save and redeploy" is enforced, not just stored: a source/runtime/entry-point edit changes the revision's image fingerprint, so the same revision-diff logic the Admin API uses for any template change cuts a real new revision (visible on the Revisions tab, traffic following it) exactly as a redeploy would.

For Python sources, Vyomi parses the code on create/update and rejects it the way a real build would fail: a syntax error or an entry point the source doesn't define returns a 400 instead of saving. Other runtimes are stored and returned as configured but not parsed.

Vyomi actually runs Python function sources on invoke (see Observability); it does not build or run an arbitrary container image, so container-deployed services and non-Python function sources are metered but not executed.

gcp.functions.services.yaml.title: YAML view of the service config
limitations: The YAML view is generated read-only from the real service state; editing and re-applying YAML directly is not simulated — use the other tabs.

gcp.functions.services.continuous_deploy.title: Continuously deploy from a repository (Cloud Build / GitHub)
limitations: Vyomi has no real GitHub/Cloud Source Repositories integration: "connect a repository" just names an owner/repo + branch against the service, and a "push" is the console's own build action rather than a real webhook.

The build step is real, not cosmetic: it parses/validates the pushed source the same way a Cloud Build step would, and only lands a new revision (visible on the Revisions tab) when that build succeeds — a broken push fails the build and leaves the service untouched, same as Source tab redeploys.
Build history (status, logs, which revision it deployed) is real per-service state, not a static list.

gcp.functions.services.triggers.title: Event triggers (Eventarc) and Cloud Build source deploys
limitations: Vyomi only has a real event source for Pub/Sub-sourced ("Custom event") triggers: creating one validates the topic exists and wires a real Pub/Sub push subscription that invokes the destination service whenever a message is published.

Eventarc providers Vyomi cannot source for real (Cloud Storage, Cloud Audit Logs, Cloud Scheduler-via-Eventarc, third-party) are rejected at trigger-create time rather than accepted and silently never firing.

gcp.functions.services.observability.title: Observability (request metrics, container instance count, logs)
limitations: Metrics (request count, request latency, container instance count) and Logs are fed by real activity — the console's own invoke calls and real Eventarc trigger deliveries — never random/synthetic data; a service nobody has called shows zeros.

Container instance count is derived from the service's minimum-instance setting and recent request activity, not a real multi-instance scheduler (Vyomi serves every request synchronously, in-process).

Request latency reflects the actual time Vyomi's sandbox spent running the function; for non-Python/container-image services (which Vyomi cannot execute) the request is still metered and logged but latency is near-zero.

gcp.functions.workerpools.crud.title: Worker pools (create, list, delete)
limitations: Worker pool instance splits across revisions are not modelled; a worker pool always runs its current template.

gcp.functions.domainmappings.crud.title: Domain mappings (map a custom domain to a service, DNS records)
limitations: Vyomi does not provision a real TLS certificate or serve traffic on the mapped domain; the DNS records it returns are illustrative.
